entries.name: Presbyterian church government: a church of courts
entries.author: reformededucation.org
entries.description: Presbyterian churches are governed by elders who meet in a series of connected courts. Here is how that works, and how it shapes the way ministers are called and ordained.

sections.heading: Government by elders
paragraphs: The word ‘Presbyterian’ comes from the Greek presbyteros, ‘elder’. A Presbyterian church is ruled neither by one bishop nor by the vote of the whole congregation, but by elders whom the congregation elects.

The Orthodox Presbyterian Church states the principle this way: “Government by presbyters or elders is a New Testament ordinance; their joint exercise of jurisdiction in presbyterial assemblies is set forth in the New Testament” (Form of Government III.2). Two features are in that sentence: rule by elders, and the elders acting together in assemblies.

sections.heading: 1. It is a church of courts
paragraphs: Presbyterians do not picture each congregation as a separate island. They picture one church, governed at several levels by courts. In the OPC there are three: the session (the elders of a local congregation), the presbytery (the elders and ministers of a region), and the general assembly, “the governing body of the whole church” (Form of Government XV.2). Some Presbyterian bodies add a synod between the presbytery and the assembly.

Each court has its own members and its own authority, and a matter can be taken from a lower court to a higher one. That is why Presbyterians often call their system connectional: the local church is a part of a larger church, and the larger church can act.

sections.heading: Teaching and ruling elders
paragraphs: In the OPC the permanent offices are teaching elder (the minister), ruling elder and deacon (Form of Government V.3). Ministers and ruling elders sit together in the courts and share in governing: “teaching elders and ruling elders” exercise jurisdiction jointly. Deacons care for the church’s mercy ministry and practical needs and do not rule.

sections.heading: 2. The congregation calls its minister
paragraphs: A Presbyterian minister is not assigned to a congregation by the denomination. The congregation chooses him. In the OPC a special committee presents a candidate and the congregation votes to issue a call (Form of Government XXII.6).

The call is not final on the congregation’s word alone. It must be approved by the presbytery before it is placed in the minister’s hands (XXII.10). The congregation chooses, and the wider church checks.

sections.heading: 3. The presbytery ordains the minister
paragraphs: Examination and ordination belong to the presbytery. The OPC says the presbytery examines candidates (Form of Government XXI.4) and that “ordination shall be performed by the body which examines the candidate” (XX.5).

A minister’s church membership reflects this. A minister belongs to the presbytery, the regional church, rather than to the congregation he serves (VI.4). The presbytery, not the local session, oversees his doctrine and conduct.

sections.heading: In short
points: A church of courts: session, presbytery and general assembly, each with authority.
The congregation calls its minister; the presbytery approves the call.
The presbytery examines and ordains him, and he is a member of the presbytery.

sections.heading: A caution
paragraphs: These details come from the OPC’s Form of Government. Other Presbyterian churches, such as the PCA, the ARP and the PC(USA), have their own books of order with their own wording, and some have an extra level such as a synod. Read the book of order of the church you are considering.

entries.name: Reformed church government: consistory, classis and synod
entries.author: reformededucation.org
entries.description: Continental Reformed churches also rule by elders, but they arrange their assemblies differently. This article explains the Church Order of Dort tradition and how it works today.

sections.heading: Where it comes from
paragraphs: Reformed church government in the Dutch and continental tradition goes back to the Church Order of Dort, adopted by the Synod of Dort in 1618–1619. Article 29 lists four kinds of assemblies: the consistory, the classical meetings (classis), the particular synods and the general synod.

Churches that follow this tradition today include the United Reformed Churches, the Canadian and American Reformed Churches, the Christian Reformed Church and others in the denominations list on this site.

sections.heading: The local church is where the keys are
paragraphs: The URCNA’s Church Order begins with “Foundational Principles of Reformed Church Government”. Principle 5 states: “The Lord gave no permanent universal, national, or regional offices to his church. The office of elder (presbyter/episkopos) is clearly local in authority and function; thus, Reformed church government is presbyterial, since the church is governed by elders, not by broader assemblies.”
Principle 6 adds that the local church is governed by Christ from heaven by his Word and Spirit, “and it is not subject to rule by sister churches who, with it, are subject to the one Christ.”

sections.heading: Broader assemblies, not higher courts
paragraphs: Reformed churches speak of broader assemblies rather than higher courts. A classis or synod brings together delegates from several churches. It does not stand above them as a separate authority. Article 84 of the Church Order of Dort says: “No church shall in any way lord it over another church, no minister over other ministers, no elder or deacon over other elders or deacons.”

Principle 7 of the URCNA’s statement says federative relationships “do not belong to the essence or being of the church” but serve its well-being, and that entering or leaving them is voluntary. Principle 9 says the assemblies’ decisions “derive their authority from their conformity to the Word of God”.
Article 24 of the URCNA Church Order says the same about congregations: they “are distinct and do not have dominion over each other”, yet they ought to seek one another’s unity and help.

sections.heading: Only the consistory continues
paragraphs: Article 16 of the URCNA Church Order names three assemblies, the consistory, the classis and the synod, and says: “Classis and synod are broader assemblies that exist only when meeting by delegation. Only the consistory is a continuing body.” The consistory is the local governing body, made up of the minister and the elders. When the deacons meet with the consistory the body is called the council (Article 23), which “shall operate under the authority of the consistory”.

sections.heading: Offices
paragraphs: The URCNA lists three offices: minister of the Word, elder and deacon (Article 1). The Church Order of Dort (Article 2) names four kinds of office: ministers, doctors (professors of theology), elders and deacons. Reformed churches distinguish the minister from the elder as separate offices, and the minister belongs to the local church’s consistory.

sections.heading: Calling and ordination
paragraphs: The URCNA Church Order (Article 6) describes the lawful calling of a new minister in three steps: the council elects a declared candidate after praying and receiving the advice of the congregation; delegates of the classis examine his doctrine and life; and he is ordained in public before the congregation, with the laying on of hands by the ministers present and by the elders of the congregation.

sections.heading: A caution
paragraphs: The URCNA’s own statement describes Reformed church government as presbyterial. The difference from the Presbyterian pattern is one of emphasis and structure, not of who rules. Other Reformed churches, such as the CanRC, the CRC and the RCUS, have their own church orders; read the one that applies.

entries.name: Presbyterian and Reformed polity compared
entries.author: reformededucation.org
entries.description: Both are governed by elders, both call ministers through the congregation and both guard the church with confessions. The differences are in the status of the wider assemblies, the minister’s membership and the way ordination works.

sections.heading: What they share
paragraphs: Presbyterian and continental Reformed churches both reject government by a single bishop and government by the congregation alone. Both are ruled by elders elected by the congregation, and both use a confession as their standard: the Westminster Standards among Presbyterians, the Three Forms of Unity among continental Reformed.

head: Question
Presbyterian (for example the OPC)
Continental Reformed (for example the URCNA)
rows: How is the church described?
One church governed by a series of courts.
Local churches united in a federation of churches, meeting in broader assemblies.
Local governing body
Session
Consistory (council)
Wider bodies
Presbytery and general assembly, both courts; some churches add a synod.
Classis and synod, described as broader assemblies.
Are the wider bodies permanent?
Presbytery is a continuing court.
Classis and synod “exist only when meeting by delegation”; only the consistory continues.
Named offices
Teaching elder (minister), ruling elder, deacon.
Minister, elder, deacon (URCNA); the Church Order of Dort also names professors.
Who calls a minister?
The congregation, by vote; the presbytery approves the call.
The council elects after the congregation’s advice; classis delegates examine him.
Who ordains?
The presbytery that examined him.
The calling church, with ministers present and the elders laying on hands, after the classis examination.
Minister’s membership
A member of the presbytery.
Serves as part of the local consistory.
Source of authority for assemblies
The courts rule with the authority of Scripture under the church’s constitution.
Decisions “derive their authority from their conformity to the Word of God”.

sections.heading: The heart of the difference
paragraphs: Presbyterians stress that the church is one and is governed in one system of courts, so a presbytery can act for the whole church in its region. Continental Reformed churches stress that the elder’s office is local, so the broader assemblies are meetings of churches that cannot rule over them.

sections.heading: How big a difference is it?
paragraphs: It is easy to overstate. The URCNA’s own principles call Reformed government ‘presbyterial’, and churches in both families share elders, confessions, discipline and a high view of the church. Some Reformed and Presbyterian bodies have worked together for decades. Still, the differences affect practice: who examines a minister, who holds him accountable, how a dispute is settled and how much authority a regional body has.

sections.heading: Sources and limits
paragraphs: The Presbyterian column follows the Orthodox Presbyterian Church’s Form of Government, and the Reformed column follows the URCNA Church Order and the Church Order of Dort. Other churches in each family differ in detail. A secondary discussion of these differences appears in a Puritan Board thread, which I used only as a pointer.

entries.name: How a minister is called and ordained: Presbyterian and Reformed compared
entries.author: reformededucation.org
entries.description: Step by step, how a pastor comes to serve a congregation in a Presbyterian church and in a continental Reformed church.

sections.heading: In a Presbyterian church (the OPC as an example)
points: The presbytery examines a man for licensure and ordination (Form of Government XXI.4).
A congregation needing a pastor forms a committee, which presents a candidate; the congregation votes to issue a call (XXII.6).
The presbytery approves the call before it is placed in his hands (XXII.10).
The presbytery ordains him: “ordination shall be performed by the body which examines the candidate” (XX.5).
He becomes a member of the presbytery and is governed by it, not by the local session alone (VI.4).

sections.heading: In a continental Reformed church (the URCNA as an example)
points: A man aspiring to the ministry is supervised by his own consistory while he trains (Article 3).
He is examined at a meeting of the classis, in the presence of his consistory, and declared a candidate (Article 4).
A calling church’s council elects him after prayer and after hearing the advice of the congregation (Article 6).
Delegates of the classis examine his doctrine and life (Article 6).
He is ordained publicly before the congregation, signs the Form of Subscription to the Three Forms of Unity, and has hands laid on him by the ministers present and by the elders (Article 6).
An ordained minister who moves to another congregation in the federation consults his current council and may accept a call only with their consent (Article 7).

sections.heading: What stands out
paragraphs: In both systems the congregation has a voice and the wider church has a check. In the Presbyterian pattern the presbytery approves the call and does the ordaining. In the Reformed pattern the classis delegates examine, but the ordination takes place in the calling church with its own elders present. Who ‘owns’ the minister differs too: the presbytery in the Presbyterian pattern, the local church in the Reformed pattern.

entries.name: Why Christian parents should not send their children to public school
entries.author: reformededucation.org
entries.description: The position of this site, with the reasons: God gives children to their parents to disciple, no school is neutral, and a school that must be secular teaches a worldview. It also says plainly where Reformed Christians disagree.

sections.heading: This is the site’s position
paragraphs: Reformed Education holds that Christian parents should not place their children in public (government) schools, and that they should choose a Christian school, a classical Christian school or home education instead. That is an editorial position of this site, stated openly. It is not a doctrine of the Westminster Standards, the Three Forms of Unity or any denomination we list.

Reformed Christians do disagree about it. Some faithful parents use public schools and some churches do not press the matter. This article gives the reasons for our view, then says what it does not claim.

sections.heading: 1. God gives the education of children to parents
paragraphs: The great Old Testament text on teaching children is addressed to parents: “And thou shalt teach them diligently unto thy children, and shalt talk of them when thou sittest in thine house, and when thou walkest by the way, and when thou liest down, and when thou risest up” (Deuteronomy 6:7, KJV). Psalm 78:5–7 says the Lord commanded the fathers to make his law known to their children, so that each generation would set its hope in God.

The New Testament gives the same charge: “ye fathers, provoke not your children to wrath: but bring them up in the nurture and admonition of the Lord” (Ephesians 6:4, KJV). The Westminster Larger Catechism, in answer 129, lists what parents and other superiors owe those under them: “to instruct, counsel, and admonish them”, and it cites Deuteronomy 6:6–7 and Ephesians 6:4 among its proofs.

Parents may use teachers, as they use doctors and pastors. But the responsibility stays with them. Choosing a school is choosing who will stand in the place of the parent for about thirty hours a week, and that choice belongs to a father and mother before God.

sections.heading: 2. No education is neutral
paragraphs: Every subject, from history to science to literature, is taught from some view of God, man and the world. A school cannot teach without assuming answers to the questions ‘What is man?’, ‘What is right?’ and ‘Where did we come from?’

A government school that serves a whole nation is in a difficult position. It cannot teach the gospel, so it teaches as if God did not matter. The Presbyterian theologian A. A. Hodge saw this coming. In lectures published in 1887 he argued that if every party has the right to remove from the public schools what it does not believe, then “he that believes most must give way to him that believes least”, until nothing is left that assumes God. He warned that, carried through consistently, “the United States system of national popular education will be the most efficient and wide instrument for the propagation of Atheism which the world has ever seen” (Popular Lectures on Theological Themes, ‘The Kingly Office of Christ’, p. 281). Hodge wrote that as a prediction of where a consistent secular system leads, not as a description of every teacher or school.

sections.heading: 3. Children are discipled by whoever spends the most time with them
paragraphs: Jesus said, “The disciple is not above his master: but every one that is perfect shall be as his master” (Luke 6:40, KJV). Children become like the people who teach them and the people they grow up among. “He that walketh with wise men shall be wise: but a companion of fools shall be destroyed” (Proverbs 13:20, KJV).

A school day puts a child for most of his waking hours among teachers and classmates whom the parents did not choose and who may share none of the family’s convictions. The Christian parent has to ask honestly who is forming the child’s loves, habits and friendships.

sections.heading: 4. The aim is more than safety
paragraphs: It is common to defend public school by saying that Christian children can be light in a dark place. There is truth in this for grown believers. But children are not sent to school to be missionaries; they are sent to be taught. Parents are told to train them first (Proverbs 22:6), and a child who is still being formed is not the best person to hold a position against a system built by adults.

The positive aim matters more than the warning. Christian education seeks to teach every subject as a part of God’s world, under Christ, with the catechism and the Scriptures as the frame for the rest. That is hard to do in a school that has to stay silent about him.

sections.heading: What this does not claim
points: It does not claim that every child in a public school will lose the faith, or that every public school teacher is an enemy. Many are kind and capable.

It does not say that Christian schools and homeschools are automatically faithful. Some are only moral or only academic, and they need the same testing. See ‘Choosing an alternative to public school’ on this site.

It does not condemn parents who have no other choice. Some families cannot afford a school or cannot teach at home. The church should help them, and they can still do most of the work of discipling at home (see ‘Parents cannot farm out their children’).
It does not settle the question for your church. Ask your elders, and compare the views of your own denomination.

sections.heading: If your children are already in public school
paragraphs: Do not panic, and do not wait. Begin family worship and catechism if you have not. Know what they are being taught and talk about it at the table. Talk to your pastor and elders, and pray about a move. Look at the options in the Education section of this site, and consider the cost, the distance, the time and the help your church can give.

entries.name: Choosing an alternative to public school
entries.author: reformededucation.org
entries.description: Four main options for Christian parents: a Christian school, a classical Christian school, home education and a hybrid. What each asks of you, and what to check before you choose.

sections.heading: Start with the aim
paragraphs: An alternative to public school is only as good as what it teaches and who teaches it. Before choosing, write down what you want: sound doctrine, a real academic education, a godly community, the time to disciple your children yourselves, or all of these. Different options give different things.

head: Option
What it is
Often a good fit when
Watch for
rows: Christian school
A school run by a church or a group of Christian families, with Christian teachers.
Both parents work, or parents want a school community and teaching from others.
Doctrine differs between schools; some are only ‘Christian’ in name. Ask for the statement of faith and read it. Tuition can be high.
Classical Christian school
A Christian school that teaches the liberal arts, Latin, logic and rhetoric and the great books.
Parents value a demanding, book-centred education with a Christian frame.
Schools range from Reformed to broadly evangelical. Membership in an association is not a guarantee of your church’s doctrine.
Home education
Parents teach, using curriculum chosen for their family.
A parent can be at home, and the family wants to teach the faith and the school day together.
It asks a great deal of one parent’s time and patience. Legal requirements vary by state and country, so check your own.
Hybrid or co-op
Children attend school or a co-op for some days and learn at home on others, or families teach one another’s children.
A family wants help with teaching but keeps the home as the centre.
Needs commitment from several families and a clear statement of what is taught.

sections.heading: Questions to ask any school or curriculum
points: What is its statement of faith, and which church or churches stand behind it?
Who teaches, and are the teachers professing Christians who are members of a church?
How does it teach history, science and literature? Ask to see the books.
How does it handle discipline, and how are parents kept involved?
What does it cost, and what help does it give to families who cannot pay? Do not assume costs; ask for current figures.
If it is a homeschool curriculum, does it fit the number of children and the time you have?

sections.heading: Finding them on this site
paragraphs: Reformed Education lists schools, school associations, curricula and teacher-training groups, and gives the doctrinal basis and points to weigh for each. Some are Reformed and some are not, and each entry says which. Start with the Education topic, then open ‘Christian Schools’ or ‘Home Education’. Where a detail is unknown the page says so, and you should confirm details with the school itself.

sections.heading: Whichever you choose
paragraphs: No school or curriculum can do the work that belongs to parents. Family worship, catechism, church and time at home are what make any of these options Christian. See ‘Parents cannot farm out their children’ on this site.

entries.name: Parents cannot farm out their children
entries.author: reformededucation.org
entries.description: Children are discipled by time with their parents, and that time cannot be handed to a school, a screen or a program. What the research does and does not show about family stability and parents’ marriage.

sections.heading: The plain point
paragraphs: Christian parents are sometimes told that if they choose the right school, church programme or curriculum, the children will be taken care of. They will not. A school can teach, and a church can teach. Neither can replace a father and a mother who are present, who talk with their children, pray with them and eat with them.

Deuteronomy 6:7 describes the pattern: the words of God are to be talked of “when thou sittest in thine house, and when thou walkest by the way, and when thou liest down, and when thou risest up” (KJV). Discipleship here is not a class. It is the ordinary hours of the day, shared.

sections.heading: What the Westminster Standards say parents owe
paragraphs: The Larger Catechism (answer 129) says superiors, and first of all parents, owe those under them love, prayer and blessing; instruction, counsel and admonition; and “protecting, and providing for them all things necessary for soul and body”, and a “grave, wise, holy, and exemplary carriage”. Nearly all of these need presence. A child cannot be instructed or given an example by someone who is not there.

sections.heading: What we can ask of a busy household
points: A meal together most days, with no screens.
Family worship: a short passage, a prayer and a catechism question. Sources for this are in the Family section of this site.
One-to-one time with each child, doing something together.
Saying no to activities that take the family out of the house every evening.
Being at church together and talking about the sermon afterwards.
Fathers especially: Ephesians 6:4 addresses fathers by name.

sections.heading: Parents’ marriage is part of their children’s education
paragraphs: Children learn what a husband and wife are by watching theirs. Ephesians 5 sets the pattern: the husband loves as Christ loved the church and the wife respects and submits to him; that marriage pictures Christ and the church. A home where the parents love each other and stay together teaches children more about the gospel than any lesson can.
Research is consistent with this, and it is worth stating carefully:

sections.heading: What the research shows, and does not show
points: Family stability is among the strongest correlates of a child’s later prospects. A study by Raj Chetty and colleagues of 40 million children (“Where is the Land of Opportunity?”, National Bureau of Economic Research, 2014) found that areas with higher upward mobility have “greater family stability”, along with less segregation, less inequality, better primary schools and more social capital. The authors wrote that the fraction of children living in single-parent households was the single strongest correlate of upward income mobility among the variables they explored, as reported by the American Enterprise Institute’s review of the work.

That research is descriptive. The authors say it does not identify the causes, and later work found the link weaker for the causal effect of a place. It is a strong association across communities, not a proof about any one child.

Parents’ relationship quality is linked to how they parent. A 2014 study in the Journal of Family Issues (Ratcliffe, Norton and Dutschi), summarized by the Institute for Family Studies, found that parents who reported an affectionate, positive relationship engaged more positively with their child two years later, and that this was linked to fewer behaviour problems in the child at age five.

We have not found a study showing that parents staying together and liking each other is the single greatest predictor of an individual child’s success, so this site does not make that claim. It is fair to say that the evidence points strongly in that direction and that it agrees with what Scripture teaches about marriage and the home.

sections.heading: For those whose marriage has ended or never was
paragraphs: Single parents and widowed, divorced or abandoned parents are not condemned by any of this, and many raise godly children. The church is told to look after widows and the fatherless (James 1:27). If you are such a parent, ask your church for help, including men to be examples for your sons and women for your daughters.

sections.heading: If your marriage is struggling
paragraphs: Talk to your pastor or elders soon, and consider biblical counseling. The Biblical Counseling section of this site lists organizations and books on marriage. If you are in danger, call your local emergency number or, in the U.S., call or text 988.
